stances.claim: The SC's reversal of the 'infamous' condonation doctrine -- only prospectively -- has been both praised and pilloried; the column will sum up the 71-page Perlas-Bernabe ponencia simply for nonlawyers

Laws passed by Congress cannot restrict the constitutionally-enshrined duty of the entire judiciary -- not just the SC -- to determine grave abuse of discretion on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the government
The OMB Law cannot restrict the CA's authority to hear Binay Jr.'s certiorari petition alleging grave abuse of discretion by the OMB -- TROs are ancillaries inherent to certiorari jurisdiction

The 1987 Constitution granted the SC sole power to promulgate rules of procedure in all courts and prohibited Congress from increasing SC appellate jurisdiction without its advice and concurrence -- the OMB Law violated both constraints
The OMB is a quasi-judicial agency, not a 'court' -- by including OMB appeals in SC appellate jurisdiction, the OMB Law unconstitutionally increased that jurisdiction without SC concurrence

The condonation doctrine traces to Pascual v. Provincial Board (Oct 31, 1959), decided under the 1935 Constitution when graft was not rampant and 'honor, integrity and delicadeza were sacred values practiced universally'

After half a century, times have changed unfortunately for the worse -- corruption has become pervasive -- and the 1987 Constitution mandates transparency, honesty, and accountability, which the condonation doctrine contradicts

Election is not a mode of condoning an administrative offense; there is simply no constitutional or statutory basis to support the notion that an official elected for a different term is fully absolved of any administrative liability arising from a prior term

The reversal is given only prospective effect because under Civil Code Art. 8, judicial decisions form part of the legal system and shall have no retroactive effect unless the contrary is provided -- CJ found no jurisprudence authorizing retroactivity for abandoned doctrines

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban summarizes for nonlawyers the 'praised and pilloried' Morales v. Court of Appeals (Nov 10, 2015) -- the SC decision reversing the 'infamous' condonation doctrine but only prospectively. The facts: on March 10, 2015, Ombudsman Conchita Carpio Morales placed Makati Mayor Jejomar Binay Jr. under six-month preventive suspension over six criminal and six administrative cases arising from alleged anomalies in the Makati Parking Building during his first term (2010-2013). On March 11, Binay Jr. challenged via CA certiorari; on March 16, the CA issued a TRO grounded in condonation -- that his 2013 reelection had condoned the prior-term anomalies. On March 25, Morales filed her SC certiorari, arguing that Sec. 14 of the OMB Law (RA 6770) bars any court from issuing TROs against OMB investigations and reserves OMB appeals exclusively to the SC; she also urged that the condonation doctrine be reversed for contravening the Constitution. The 71-page 'superbly written' Perlas-Bernabe ponencia, concurred in fully by eight magistrates (including CJ Sereno and Senior Justice Carpio), partly by one (Bersamin), with four taking no part and one on leave, is a scholarly dissertation summarized as follows. First, on CA jurisdiction: laws passed by Congress cannot restrict the constitutionally-enshrined duty of the entire judiciary (not just the SC) to determine grave abuse of discretion on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the government; ergo, the OMB Law cannot restrict the CA from hearing Binay Jr.'s certiorari petition alleging grave abuse by the OMB, and TROs are 'mere regulatory processes' ancillary to certiorari. Moreover, the 1987 Constitution grants the SC sole rule-making power and prohibits Congress from increasing SC appellate jurisdiction without its advice and concurrence -- the OMB Law violated both by routing all OMB appeals exclusively to the SC; further, since the OMB is a quasi-judicial agency, not a 'court,' the OMB Law unconstitutionally expanded SC appellate jurisdiction. Second, on condonation: the Court traced the doctrine to Pascual v. Provincial Board (Oct 31, 1959), decided under the 1935 Constitution when graft was not rampant and 'honor, integrity and delicadeza were sacred values practiced universally.' After more than half a century, times have changed for the worse; corruption has become pervasive; the 1987 Constitution mandates transparency, honesty, and accountability. After thorough review, the Court held: 'Election is not a mode of condoning an administrative offense, and there is simply no constitutional or statutory basis ... to support the notion that an official elected for a different term is fully absolved of any administrative liability arising from an offense done during a prior term.' Nonetheless, abandonment is given only prospective effect because under Civil Code Art. 8, judicial decisions form part of the legal system and shall have no retroactive effect unless otherwise provided -- CJ tried researching but found no jurisprudence authorizing retroactivity for abandoned doctrines. In sum: the CA has jurisdiction over OMB administrative rulings, and henceforth condonation by reelection can no longer be used as a defense. Postscript: on Oct 9, 2015, the OMB dismissed Binay Jr. from office, mooting his CA petition.
